newsitem.title: KUWAIT: INTERVIEW-Kuwait bourse ready for futures trade.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Kuwait bourse ready for futures trade.

text.p: The Kuwait Stock Exchange, the liveliest in the Arab world, is ready for the next step: futures trading to be followed by an opening up to all foreign investors, the head of the bourse said on Tuesday.
"We are ready for it," KSE Director-General Hisham al-Oteibi told Reuters of plans to introduce futures trading by investment portfolio managing institutions.
"It is a matter of timing and priorities...Not all the backup systems for futures trading are in place yet," he added of the awaited move which was approved by the Commerce Ministry late last year.

Futures trading "is the natural trend for the evolution of the market" which has been setting new records this week, triggering concern by some experts that the rise could be driven in some cases by heavy speculation and not fudamentals.

On Tuesday, the KSE index closed lower than Saturday's record of 2354.7 points at 2,334.3 -- a 22.5 percent rise from the start of 1997 -- while trading value and volume were lower than Monday's records but higher than last week's daily average.
The value soared on Monday to 125.8 million dinars ($414 million) during the 2-1/2-hour session in which 445 million shares were traded.
The index rose by about 40 percent a year in 1996 and 1995.
"Normally after a rise there are correction moves," Oteibi said. "They are always a possibility and are expected but not a crash...No way, impossible."
The word crash revives memories of the collapse of Souq al- Manakh unofficial exchange in 1982, resulting in a debt of over $20 billion which the government is still trying to resolve.

The government at the time stepped in to buy shares in many concerns which it is now selling in the first phase of a privatisation programme that would eventually include the more complex, heavily-susidised public utilities.
Oteibi said that an expert committee was working to complete this year recommendations to amend laws to allow foreign investors in line with World Trade Organisation (WTO) rules.
The tiny, oil-rich Gulf Arab state is a WTO member.
"We should open it up," he added. "It will give the market more depth, transparency and added credibility...It will also bring know-how, a very good data base and analytical base."
He advised small as well as large investors "to be educated and read the financial data which we and listed firms issue and base decisions accordingly, not following speculators."

Although trading on the KSE is open only to nationals of Oman, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar experts say trading value on the KSE was four times higher than the total for seven other official Arab bourses.
It is probably twice the size if the exchanges of fellow Gulf Arab Saudi Arabia and the UAE were included, they add.
Kuwait's foreign residents can trade through mutual funds.
In 1996 trading value on the KSE, which currently has some 65 listed firms with a market capitalisation of about $24 billion, was $19.2 billion, a daily average under $100 billion.
The value in Saudi Arabia, the region's biggest economy and the world's largest oil exporter and producer, was $6.8 billion.
